Core Structure-Oriented Asymmetric α‑Allenylic Alkylation of Amino
Acid Esters Enabled by Chiral Aldehyde/Palladium Catalysis
Hao Zhang, Wei Wen,* Ze-Xi Lu, Zhu-Lian Wu, Tian Cai, and Qi-Xiang Guo*

ABSTRACT: Aiming at the reported chiral synthons leading to
manzacidins A and D, here we report a highly efficient catalytic
asymmetric α-allenylic alkylation reaction of NH
2
-unprotected
amino acid esters that is promoted by combined chiral aldehyde/
palladium catalysis. Fifty examples of unnatural α,α-disubstituted
amino acid esters are reported with good-to-excellent yields and
stereoselectivities. Based on this methodology, a key intermediate
leading to manzacidin C and its other three stereoisomers is
prepared accordingly.
M
anzacidins are important members of the bromopyrrole
alkaloid family.
1
Because of their broad biological
activities and unique tetrahydropyrimidine cores, they have
attracted significant attention from synthetic chemists.
2
The
tetrahydropyrimidine cores of manzacidins feature chiral 1,3-
tertiary-quaternary carbon centers and C-6 epimers. Therefore,
the precise construction of these chiral units is an essential
prerequisite to the preparation of the corresponding natural
products. In 2000, Ohfune and co-workers reported the first
total synthesis of manzacidins A and C.
3
Subsequently, various
elegant asymmetric methods�including the use of chiral
synthons,
4
chiral auxiliaries,
5
and chiral catalysts
6
�have been
reported for the preparation of manzacidins and their
analogues. However, the majority of reported methods rely
on the use of stoichiometric amounts of chiral reagents with
few catalytic asymmetric routes. Therefore, highly efficient
catalytic asymmetric methodologies for the construction of the
corresponding chiral tetrahydropyrimidine core are required.
In Ohfune’s work, chiral tetrahydropyrimidine I and its
precursor tetrahydropyrimidine-2-one II are two intermediates
that lead to manzacidin C.
3
Intermediate II was prepared from
the chiral synthon (S)-2-aminopent-4-en-1-ol in seven steps.
We envisaged that the carboxyl group of II could be prepared
by oxidizing the corresponding alkene double bonds of III and
that the chiral tetrahydropyrimidine-2-one core of III could be
constructed by the asymmetric intramolecular addition of the
NH group to the allene unit of compound IV.
7
Chiral urea−
allene IV could be readily prepared by the addition of amino
acid ester V to 4-methylbenzenesulfonyl isocyanate.
8
Thus,
allene-containing chiral amino acid ester V was anticipated to
be the key starting material for the preparation of manzacidin
C and its family members. We envisaged that this amino acid
ester could be prepared by the catalytic asymmetric α-allenylic
alkylation of amino acid ester derivatives (Figure 1a).
The catalytic asymmetric α-allenylic alkylation of amino acid
ester derivatives is an important strategy for the preparation of
chiral amino acids
9
or chiral allenes.
10
Especially, Zhang,
Wang, and several other research groups reported their elegant
methods for constructing chiral amino acid molecules bearing
both carbon and axial chiralities.
11
However, all reported
methods employ N-protected amino acid esters as reactants.
Chiral aldehyde catalysis can be used to promote the direct α-
functionalization of N-unprotected amino acid derivatives.
12
In
our previous work, we explored both chiral aldehyde-mediated
organocatalysis
13
and combined organo/transition-metal cat-
alysis.
14
In particular, we reported a chiral aldehyde-involved
ternary catalysis that promoted the asymmetric α-allylation
15
and α-benzylation
16
of NH
2
-unprotected amino acid deriva-
tives. With the utilization of this reported reaction model,
15
we
reasoned that the straightforward synthesis of the target allene-
contained chiral amino acid ester 3 from the racemic reactants
1 and 2 with high efficiency via a dynamic kinetic asymmetric
transformation (DyKAT) process
11a
could be achieved.
Furthermore, the absolute configuration of the chiral
quaternary carbon center might be easily switched by changing
the chiral configuration of the catalyst, thereby providing an

Increasing the equivalents of amino acid ester 1a increased the
yield of 3a to 59% (Table 1, entry 17). By employing ZnBr

ligand L6 was reinvestigated. Using ligand L6, the yield, dr,
and ee all improved relative to catalyst L5 under equivalent
conditions (Table 1, entry 22). Next, the reaction temperature
and the equivalents of Lewis acid were tuned (see the
Supporting Information). When this reaction proceeded at 15
°C and with 60 mol % Lewis acid ZnBr
2
, product 3a was
generated in 83% yield, 95:5 dr, and >99% ee (Table 1, entry
24). A comparison experiment indicated that the R-
configuration of chiral aldehyde CA-1 matched with the S-
configuration of chiral phosphine ligand L6 (Table 1, entries
24 and 25). Based on these results, the reaction conditions
listed in Table 1, entry 24, were chosen as the optimal
conditions for subsequent investigations.
With the optimal reaction conditions established, we set out
to complete the formal synthesis of manzacidin C and
construct core tetrahydropyrimidine-2-one II with various
chiral configurations. The synthetic route to manzacidin C is
shown in Figure 2a. Under the optimal reaction conditions,
chiral aldehyde ent-CA-1 and ligand ent-L6 catalyzed the
formation of (S,R)-3a in 83% yield, 95:5 dr, and 99% ee. After
(S,R)-3a was reacted with 4-methylbenzenesulfonyl isocyanate,
product 4 was obtained in 90% yield. Next, the intramolecular
addition of the amino group to the allene unit was studied.
After various reaction conditions were screened (see the
Supporting Information), rhodium catalysis was found to give
the product, (S,S)-5, in 79% yield and 55:45 dr. This
diastereoisomeric mixture was treated with magnesium under
sonication, leading to (S,S)-6 in 79% yield. The major
diastereoisomer of (S,S)-6 was isolated by silica column
chromatography and submitted to subsequent oxidation/
reduction reactions, affording (S,S)-7 in 82% yield. Finally,

Ohfune intermediate (S,S)-8 in 72% yield. The analytic data of
(4S,6S)-8 was identical to that reported in the literature, and
the absolute configuration was assigned by comparing its
optical rotation with literature values (see the Supporting
Information).
3
Thus, the catalytic asymmetric formal synthesis
of manzacidin C was achieved by using readily available and
inexpensive starting materials.
Next, the synthetic route for the preparation of (4R,6S)-8
was studied. The R configuration of the chiral quaternary
carbon center was successfully installed by using chiral
aldehyde CA-1 and chiral phosphine ligand L6 (Figures 2b
and 3a). In the preparation of chiral Ohfune intermediate
(S,S)-8, the S-configuration of the quaternary carbon center
induced the S-configuration of the chiral C-6 carbon center
under rhodium catalysis. Thus, we needed to find an
alternative reaction condition to construct the chiral C-6
carbon center with an S-configuration under induction of the R
quaternary carbon center. Fortunately, we found that
palladium catalysis could promote the generation of (4R,6S)-
5 from compound 4. Under the same manipulations used for
the synthesis of (4S,6S)-8, (4R,6S)-8 was successfully prepared
(Figure 2b).
Considering the different stereoselectivities of the rhodium
and palladium catalysts in the intramolecular hydroamination
reaction, we reasoned that the preparation of another two
isomers of compound 5 could be achieved by switching the
starting materials and catalytic systems. As expected, (4S,6R)-5
was generated from reactant ent-4 using palladium catalysis,
and the major component (4R,6R)-5 was generated from 4
under rhodium catalysis (Figure 2c). The absolute config-
uration of (4S,6R)-6 was established by single crystal X-ray
diffraction analysis, and the absolute configurations of the
other isomers of 5 were deduced from their
1
H NMR data and
the original chiral induction sources. Thus, all four stereo-
isomers of core tetrahydropyrimidine-2-one 5 were successfully
prepared using our catalytic asymmetric methodology.
Next, the application of these optimal reaction conditions to
other substituted amino acid esters and allenyl alcohol esters
was studied. First, various readily available amino acid
derivatives were employed as donors in the reaction. Amino
acid esters bearing different alkoxyl groups were well-tolerated
in the reaction, affording the corresponding products in good
yields, good diastereoselectivities, and excellent enantioselec-
tivities (Figure 3a, 3b and 3c). These results indicated that the
target products could be converted to the corresponding
amino acids under various hydrolysis conditions. Linear and
branched alkyl-substituted amino acid esters were then tested;
all of these substrates afforded products in good-to-high yields
and excellent stereoselectivities (Figure 3a, 3e−3k). The
phenylalanine ester and its analogues were also suitable

products 3l−3p with good experimental outcomes. Other
functional groups, such as an alkene, a thioether, a sulfoxide,
and a carboxylic ester, were also tolerated under the optimal
reaction conditions, giving the desired products 3q−3t in
moderate-to-high yields and excellent stereoselectivities.
Furthermore, we found the model reaction could be carried
out in a 1.0 mmol scale, leading to product 3a in 68% yield
(167.0 mg), 84:16 dr, and 94% ee (Figure 3, 3a).
The substrate scope of the allenyl alcohol esters was also
investigated. Phenyl-substituted allenylic alcohol esters bearing
a single substituent on the benzene ring were good reaction
partners for 1a. The substitution positions and the electronic
and steric effects of the substituent did not affect the
experimental outcomes. Products 3u−3ah were generated in
good-to-high yields with excellent diastereoselectivities and
enantioselectivities. Similar results were obtained when phenyl-
substituted allenylic alcohol esters bearing two substituents
were used (Figure 3b, 3ai−3ao). Nonphenyl aryl-substituted
allenylic alkylation substrates, such as naphthyl- and thionyl-
substituted ones, also reacted smoothly with 1a under the
optimal reaction conditions, giving products 3ap−3ar in
satisfactory yields and excellent stereoselectivities. Several
alkyl-substituted allenylic alcohol esters were then tested, all
of which afforded the corresponding products in high yields,
good diastereoselectivities, and excellent enantioselectivities
(Figure 3b, 3as−3ax). When a glutamate diester was used,
allenylic alkylation and lactamization took place successively,
leading to the corresponding optically active γ-lactam
derivatives with good experimental outcomes (Figure 3b,
3aw and 3ax).
Under the influence of chiral aldehyde CA-1 and chiral
ligand L6, the Schiff base 9 reacted with 2a and gave product
10 in 91% yield. After hydrolysis and protection of the amino
group by acetyl, compound 12 was prepared. The absolute
configuration of the chiral allene unit of molecule 12 was
assigned as S by comparing its optical rotation value with the
literature’s data.
10a
Combining with the quaternary S
configuration determined in (4S,6R)-6, the absolute config-
urations of the product 3a were assigned as (2R,5S) (Scheme
1). The absolute configurations of the other products were
assigned accordingly.
In conclusion, we rationally designed an asymmetric α-
allenylic alkylation reaction of NH
2
-unprotected amino acid
esters and allenylic alcohol esters. This reaction, which allows
efficient access to the key reported intermediate in the total
synthesis of manzacidin C, uses a combined catalytic system of
a chiral aldehyde, a palladium catalyst, and a Lewis acid. A
series of α,α-disubstituted amino acid derivatives were
generated with good-to-excellent experimental outcomes.
Based on this methodology, the formal synthesis of manzacidin
C and the stereodivergent synthesis of the chiral tetrahy-
dropyrimidine-2-one core structures are achieved with high
efficiency.
